name: Misspelling pairs
notes: Hand-authored pairs of (what a person typed, what they meant). Every row is a mistake somebody plausibly makes: a finger one key over, a letter Hebrew writes two ways, a sound that maps onto more than one letter, a doubled key, a missing one. Nothing here was manufactured to fill a class — where a class is thin it is thin, and README.md says which ones and why. The pairs marked `documented` in their note are already named somewhere in this repo (`.claude/rules/suggestion-bar.md`, `Bar/typing/corpus.json`, `Bar/typing/sweep/words.json`) and are here so this instrument and those agree about the same words. `class` is checked mechanically by expand.py wherever the class has a shape, so a mislabelled row fails the run rather than quietly widening a column.

taxonomy.adjacent-1: One substitution by a physically neighbouring key, derived from the rows this keyboard actually draws.
taxonomy.adjacent-2: Two neighbouring-key substitutions in one word, usually the whole hand sitting one key over.
taxonomy.transpose: Two letters swapped. Compared with final forms folded, because swapping the last two letters of a Hebrew word also changes the shape of one of them.
taxonomy.final-form: A word ending in the ordinary shape of a letter that must take its final shape.
taxonomy.final-form-wrong: A final shape used in the middle of a word, normally because a suffix was added to a word whose singular ends in one.
taxonomy.mater-drop: A dropped mater lectionis (י, ו, א) or a dropped half of a doubled vav. Hebrew is written both with and without these, and this is the commonest Hebrew misspelling there is.
taxonomy.mater-add: A mater lectionis that should not be there, almost always a second yod.
taxonomy.homophone: Letters that sound identical in modern Israeli Hebrew: א/ה/ע, ח/כ, ט/ת, כ/ק, ס/ש. A spelling error rather than a typing error.
taxonomy.omit: A missing letter that is not a mater and not half of a double.
taxonomy.double: A letter typed twice that should appear once, or once where it should appear twice.
taxonomy.clitic: A typo behind one of Hebrew's glued prefixes (ה ב ל מ ו ש כ), so the corrector is tested through the morphology layer rather than beside it.
taxonomy.phonetic: An English word spelled the way it sounds.
taxonomy.apostrophe: A contraction typed without its apostrophe.
taxonomy.must-not-correct: A correctly spelled real word. `typed` and `intended` are the same string, and committing anything else is the failure.

pairs.note: ד and ג are neighbours on the home row and בסדר is among the most typed words in Israeli chat, so this is the single likeliest one-key slip in the language.
ש sits immediately left of ד; a finger landing one key over on a very common word.
Same ש/ד slip in a word people type dozens of times a day.
ז is the key left of ס on the bottom row, and סליחה opens a message often enough that the slip shows up at the very start of the text.
ד sits directly under ר, which is the vertical slip rather than the horizontal one; the two rows offset by nothing at this column.
ן and ם are neighbours on the top row, so the two final forms are one key apart and a word ending in one very easily ends in the other.
ג/כ on the home row. פגישה is calendar vocabulary and gets typed under time pressure.
ע/כ on the home row.
ץ is the key right of ת, so the slip also lands on a final form in final position, which is exactly where a final form is legal and therefore where nothing about its shape looks wrong.
ם is the key left of פ, so this one slip produces a final mem in the middle of a word: it is a fat finger and an orthographic impossibility at the same time.
כ/ע on the home row; the corpus already knows מכונית as the word whose fourth letter is one substitution from נכון.
א/ט on the top row.
ד/ג on the home row, and the slip lands on תוגה, a real Hebrew word meaning sorrow. The hardest shape there is for any corrector: nothing about the result is misspelled.
The report that started this work. Both slips are one key in the same direction on the top row (א→ט, ו→ן), which is what a hand sitting one key over produces rather than two independent accidents.
ק→ר and ש→ד are both one key in the same direction, the same displaced-hand shape as the row above.
ש→ד and ו→ן, again both one key the same way.
מ→נ and ס→ז, the hand one key over in the other direction on the bottom row.
כ→ע and נ→מ. Two rows, one displacement.

Documented: the corpus has it and this repo's rules record that Apple's Hebrew checker calls תדוה a perfectly good word, so the fix is offered and deliberately not committed. The commonest Hebrew transposition there is.

Documented, and the same trap as תדוה: שלמו is a real verb form (they paid), so the checker vouches for the typo. Swapping the last two letters also un-finals the mem, which is why the class test folds shapes before comparing.
The final ו/י pair of עכשיו is transposed constantly; the two letters are adjacent in the word and near each other on the keyboard.
Swapping the last two letters of a word is the commonest transposition shape, because the two keys are pressed closest together in time.
י/ח transposed mid-word.
פ/ש transposed. אפשר is one of the words a request is built out of, so the slip is common and the word is short enough that no completion helps.
ד/י transposed, which is the standard way the plural ending gets scrambled.
ע/ד transposed.

Documented: named in this repo's rules as the case the Hebrew final-form correction exists for. The ordinary mem and the final mem are different keys, so a word finished in a hurry finishes on the wrong one.
Documented. Also the case the seed gate protects: צריכ still continues to צריכים, so the engine is asked to tell a finished word spelled wrong from a word on its way somewhere.
Documented; one of the 66 seed words ending in a final form.
Documented; same.
נכון is the one-word answer to half the messages anybody sends, so it is typed fast and finished carelessly.
Long enough that the final key is pressed after the eye has already moved on.
Every masculine plural ends in ים, so this one slip is available on a very large fraction of all Hebrew nouns.
Three letters, so the four-letter autocorrect gate cannot commit anything here by design. It is in the corpus to keep the offered column honest about short words rather than to be fixed.
You know the word as דרך, you add the plural, and the kaf keeps the shape you know it in. This is a knowledge slip rather than a finger slip and it is the commonest way a final form lands mid-word.
Same mechanism on כסף.
Same mechanism on צריך, which is the form people meet first and far more often than the plural.
Same mechanism on בן.
The plural of דוגמה keeps an א nobody hears, so it is dropped constantly. Same word as the flagship adjacent-2 pair, reached by the other of the two roads.
אמתי is the unvocalised spelling and אמיתי is the one modern Hebrew writes; both look right to a reader, which is why the drop survives proofreading.
One of the most misspelled words in Israeli writing; the first yod is silent and gets dropped.
The ו of מכונית carries no consonant and disappears when the word is typed quickly.
Written both ways in real life; שיעור is the standard modern spelling.
A consonantal vav in the middle of a word is written twice, and loanwords are where that rule is broken most: one vav is what almost everybody types.
The extra yod is added by analogy with words that really do carry two, and בעיה is common enough that the wrong spelling is a familiar sight.
Same doubled yod, same reason.
Work vocabulary, written with two yods by most people and with one by the Academy. If the corrector cannot leave it alone this row is worth reading twice before calling it a defect.
א and ע are the same sound in modern Israeli Hebrew, so a word spelled from its sound can start with either.
ח and כ are both the same fricative for most speakers.
Same ח/כ confusion, this time behind a ל, so the word is also longer than the four-letter gate.
ט and ת are identical in speech and a loanword has no root to appeal to, so nothing but memory picks between them.
Same ט/ת.
כ and ק are the same sound; קצת is short and extremely common.
ש here is a sin, pronounced exactly like ס, and this is the classic sin/samekh error.
ת/ט again, in a word whose root offers no help to anybody who has not studied it.
A repeated letter shape (נ twice with one letter between) invites the eye to skip one; on a phone the key can also simply not register.
A dropped middle letter in a word people type constantly; the ח carries no vowel of its own here, so nothing in the rhythm of typing marks its absence.
A missed key in the middle of a word typed several times a day.
The last letter of a short word never lands because the thumb is already on the space bar. Three letters, so the four-letter gate cannot commit here either.
The word the sweep already uses to probe the clitic readings, one letter short of finished.
Key bounce on a repeated tap: the vav is registered twice.
The word already opens with two bets, so a third is invisible while typing.
Key bounce.
Key bounce on the last letter, which is where a finger lingers before the space bar.
A one-key slip (ו/י are neighbours across two rows) behind the ב of בעבודה, so the corrector has to strip a clitic and fix a letter at once.
A dropped mater behind two stacked clitics: the control this repo's commit gate is measured against, with a real misspelling inside it.
The א/ה ending confusion behind a ל.
A doubled נ behind the two-letter clitic כש, which is the reading this repo describes as assuming as much as it rests on.
The דרך plural slip with a ב in front of it, so the mid-word final form is now two letters deep.
A final-form miss at the end of a word carrying two clitics.
ד/ג neighbours behind מה.
ר with ד directly under it, behind a ב.
j is the key right of h, and `the` is the most typed word in English, so this is the commonest single slip there is.
k/l, and the slip is on the last letter where the finger is already moving to the space bar.
n/m on the bottom row.
o/p, on a word long enough that the slip is not seen before the message is sent.
a/s on the home row.
o/p again, this time on a four-letter word, which is the shortest input the commit gate will act on at all.
y/u on the top row.
t→y and h→j, both one key right: the classic whole-hand displacement, and the reason `yjis` is a recognisable string to anybody who types.
a→s and s→d, both one key right on the home row.
o→p and g→h, two independent slips in one word rather than a displaced hand.
Documented: the repo's own example of a transposition the space bar does commit, through the neighbour rule rather than through length.
Documented; the i-before-e rule broken in the word people quote it about.
Same ie/ei swap.
Three letters, so this one is out of the commit gate's reach by design and is here for the offered column.
One of the most frequently misspelled common words in English.
The silent h after w goes missing, helped by the fact that `wich` looks pronounceable.
A dropped vowel in a word typed fast.
The unstressed middle vowel is not heard, so it is not typed.
Nobody pronounces the second b either.
The word most often cited as the hardest common English spelling: two doubles, and people usually get one of them.
A missing double at the front of a very common word.
The consonant-doubling rule before -ing is applied inconsistently by most writers.
The other direction: a double added by analogy with `till`, which really does carry one.

Documented in this repo's rules as one of the two English same-length substitutions the commit path deliberately allows. The middle vowel is a schwa, so the spelling has to be remembered rather than heard.
Documented, same reason, and consistently near the top of every list of commonly misspelled English words.
-ance and -ence sound the same unstressed.
Same -ant/-ent pair, helped along by the French spelling.
-ar spelled -er because that is what it sounds like, in a word people type when arranging things.
Documented; the apostrophe is on the numbers plane, so on a phone leaving it out is not laziness but two extra taps.
Documented as a contraction that stays in the table even though `cant` is also an ordinary English word.
Same two-extra-taps argument.
Also needs the capital, so a pass here is two corrections rather than one.
Documented as staying in the contraction table despite having an ordinary reading.
`wont` is a real English word, which is what makes this one a real decision rather than a lookup.
Documented: the sweep records this committing from the contraction table at two letters, which is below every length gate and is deliberate.
The two-letter answer to half the messages in Hebrew. Anything that replaces it is the `I` -> `idea` regression in another language.
The other one, and it is also a seed row target for the Hebrew sentence override, which is the rule most likely to overwrite it.
Three letters, extremely common, and one edit from several other real words.
The correctly spelled half of the תדוה pair above: a build that fixes the typo by rewriting anything near it fails here.
The correctly spelled control for the three עכשיו typo rows.
How Hebrew writes the loanword `app`, with an ordinary pe at the end on purpose. This repo records an over-eager final-form rule turning it into אף (nose).
The same loanword shape one letter longer; recorded as having been destroyed as קליף by the same rule.
Cabbage: a legitimate but much rarer word one homophone edit from קרוב (near/relative). The context says somebody bought it, which is exactly the signal a corrector should be reading.
Fact: a real word that is a transposition of עבודה (work), which is far commoner. A corrector that treats transpositions as slips without checking the dictionary eats this.
An acquaintance: one homophone edit from מחר (tomorrow), which is in the seed list and is much commoner.
Shipped in SharedStore.shippedPersonalDictionary. This repo records autocorrect committing it as ספא before the dictionary was read at all.

Shipped in the personal dictionary spelled with the maqaf U+05BE and typed here with the ASCII hyphen, which is the only one a Hebrew layout offers. The fold between the two is what makes the entry reachable by its owner.
One edit from `but`, which is an order of magnitude commoner.
One edit from `car`, and this repo records the first version of the neighbour rule quietly turning one into the other.
Documented: `id` was taken out of the contraction table because `That's a good id` was committing as `That's a good I'd`. Corpus nc-02.
Documented: `were` was deliberately never put into the contraction table, because it has an ordinary reading and this context is it.
One transposition from `from`, which is far commoner, and the context makes the intended word unambiguous.
The correctly spelled half of the recieve pair: a build that corrects on sight rather than on evidence fails here.
Shipped in the personal dictionary; recorded as having been committed as `Nit` on a stock install before anything read that list.
Shipped in the personal dictionary; recorded as having been committed as `Handing`. The same `Hi ` context the rules use for it.
Shipped in the personal dictionary, and the entry that owned the first seven letters of `keyboard` until the rule about extending a common word was written. Typed in full it must simply survive.
